_about: Per-metric change thresholds shared by the maintainer dashboard (the
THRESHOLDS constant in index.html, which test_kernel_checks_page.py keeps
equal to this file) and pr_report.py. A change of at least `pct` percent of
the previous value counts: the page colors it, the report lists it. A
metric this file doesn't name takes 10%; one it names without `pct` has no
percentage test, only `abs`. With `mad`, it must also exceed that many times
the larger of the two runs' median absolute deviations (the ± at the
start of a kernel row's range, the "MAD d"
of a component's), so a noisy case does not flag its own jitter. With `abs`,
it must also be at least that much in the metric's unit, so a stage of a
fraction of a second does not flag tens of milliseconds. From a zero
baseline only `abs` decides, so a count that should flag 0 -> 1 takes
`abs` 1. A `neutral` metric is shown but never counted better or worse.
`gated` metrics are the regressions a report leads with; a `derived` metric
repeats another and is not compared. Only an `across_parts` metric is compared between runs on
different parts of one NPU generation (Strix and Krackan, or the CPU a
CPU-only check ran on): the others are host time, which moves with the
machine. Kernel object size is the code and data the tested entry point
reaches, not the harness, its siblings or the runtime image.
In two nightlies of one commit, cycles moved by well under 1%, dispatch_us
(then published as npu_us) by 17% at the 90th percentile on npu1, where one
case's MAD was 21% of its median. npu_us, the dispatch less an empty one's
median, keeps that rule with a 2 us floor: a small kernel's is a few us. The
empty dispatch itself (dispatch_overhead_us) is the host's and the runtime's,
not the kernel's, so it is shown but not judged.
The rest are the component checks'. In three back-to-back runs of one commit
on an npu2, mobilenet's per-image times moved by up to 3.8%, its
end-to-end time by 6.4% and its compile time by 3.7%; its compile's peak RSS,
over three cold compiles of one seed and batch, moved by 1.6%. The warm compile
(same cache_dir, right after the cold one) has not had its own variance measured
yet; its thresholds below match the cold ones' until it has. In three sweeps,
every seed's placement cost was identical, the mean CPU time moved by 1.6%, the
slowest seed's by 18%, and peak memory by under 1%; the sweep runs on shared
hosted runners, so CPU time has room. The allocator's corpus is fixed, and two
full runs gave identical bank sharing. The router's corpus is new each night:
over three nightly seed ranges per device, hops over the constructed routing
moved by at most 0.2% and msels per design by 4.6%. The allocator's wall time
moved by 36% and the router's time per design by 41% with the machine's load.
Failure counts take `abs` 1: any change counts, from zero too.
Llama 3.2 1B's decode: tokens per second moves like a time, so it takes
us_per_image's 5% (higher_is_better flips which way is worse); time per
token and the ratio over the DMA floor are derived from it, the floor being
fixed by the configuration. Its artifact sizes move only when the compile
does, like kernel object size. These llama thresholds are provisional: two
runs so far, so their run-to-run variance is not measured yet.
A compile's stage times (compile_<stage>_s, from aiecc's --profile-json, and
the time outside aiecc) take compile_s's 15%; provisional, measured so far
only on compile-only runs, not over several nightlies. Every compile time
takes a 0.5 s floor.
The whole compile's peak memory (every process together, its user scope's
memory.peak) takes the largest process's 10% until its own spread is measured.
YOLO26n's detector: time per image at batch 1 and at batch 8, end to end,
its dispatch and its NPU time (the dispatch less its full ELF's empty
dispatch), takes us_per_image's 5%, and its host overhead (the end-to-end
call less the dispatch) host_overhead_us_per_image's 10%, each with the
same MAD rule. Each frame rate is derived from its time, and
its full ELF's size moves only when the compile does. Images matching the
oracle count like tokens_passed; images
matching onnxruntime are information only (the oracle decides pass or fail)
and take the same 1%, neutral. Since all 128 images, map50_coco128's mAP@0.5
against coco128's own labels, should reproduce bit for bit night to night
(the device's detections are already gated bit-exact against the oracle);
0.001 absolute, gated, is a regression floor, not a measured spread. Its
page tab also shows the fp32 ONNX model's own mAP50 on the same images as a
fixed reference line (0.6365), computed once offline, not from a nightly run.
generate.py's time to first token and decode rate are one run each, so they
take 10%; its prompt rate is derived from the time to first token, and its
greedy agreement counts like tokens_passed. Provisional: no nightly of
YOLO26n or of generate.py has run yet.
Each kernel's error, per output dtype, against the correctly rounded
function: any rise of 1 ulp, or of 0.1 percentage points not correctly
rounded, is an accuracy regression, gated like cycles. MobileNet's NPU time
per image is its dispatch less the same night's empty-dispatch baseline, and
its host overhead the end-to-end call less the dispatch; both take its
per-image time's rule.
